notes.meaning: The heading names a tune, and David cries out that God feels far away. Yet he still calls Him 'my God' twice, so his faith holds on even when God seems silent. Jesus prayed these first words on the cross (Matthew 27:46). There he carried our sins and felt God's anger against sin, yet he still called the Father his God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: A Catholic reading stresses that the Father never stopped loving the Son and their union was never broken. Here 'forsaken' means God let Christ's human nature suffer fully without rescuing him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have doubted that David wrote this psalm. They have dated it much later, to Jeremiah's time, the exile in Babylon, or after that.

notes.meaning: He prays day and night, but no answer comes and his heart finds no rest. Even so, he keeps crying out to 'my God.' Jesus also prayed through the night in the garden and through the day on the cross. Unanswered prayer is a reason to keep praying, not to give up.

Even in the dark, he refuses to blame God. God is holy, which means He is pure and always right in what He does. He is pictured as a king seated on a throne made of His people's songs of praise. Because God is like this, the sufferer need not lose hope.

He remembers Israel's ancestors. Again and again they trusted God, cried to Him, and were rescued. No one who truly hoped in God was ever put to shame. The same faithful God gives him a reason to hope now.

He feels lower than a man, like a worm people step on without a thought. Everyone mocks him and looks down on him. Christians see this fulfilled in Jesus, who made himself low and was despised for our sake.

differ.view: These words fit Christ's shame on the cross even better than they fit David.
These words best express David's own sense of being small and unworthy. It is hard to see how Jesus would use them of himself.

notes.meaning: Onlookers laugh at him, sneer and shake their heads. They mock his faith: 'He trusts the LORD, so let the LORD save him!' At the cross people did these very things and said almost these very words (Matthew 27:39, 43). Without meaning to, the mockers admitted that Jesus trusted God.

Against the mockers, he points back to his birth. God brought him safely out of the womb, kept him safe as a nursing baby, and has been his God from his first day. For Jesus, God watched over his birth in a stable and his escape from Herod. The God who cared for us then will not drop us now.

Now he makes his plea in plain words: 'Do not stay far away.' Trouble is close, and no one else can help. This was true for Jesus when his disciples ran away. When every other help fails, God is the one who helps.

His enemies surround him like huge bulls from Bashan, a rich grazing land east of the Jordan River. They open their mouths like roaring lions ready to tear their prey. They are proud and cruel, more like beasts than men. At the cross, these were the powerful leaders who plotted against Jesus.

Now he describes his body. His strength is spilled out like water, his bones feel pulled apart, and his heart melts like wax. He is as dry as broken pottery, his tongue sticks to his mouth, and he lies near death. These words match the cross: the stretched body, the burning thirst (John 19:28), and the death God allowed for our sake.

differ.view: Here is a picture of Christ dying on the cross under the weight of our sin.
These lines describe the deepest human distress and fit David. They should not be pressed as an exact picture of Christ's own sufferings.

notes.meaning: His enemies circle him like a pack of wild street dogs, a gang of evil men. Then comes a striking line: 'they have pierced my hands and feet.' This never happened to David, but it happened to Jesus when he was nailed to the cross. Christians have long seen it as a clear prophecy of the crucifixion, a kind of death the Jews did not use.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many printed Hebrew Bibles read 'like a lion, my hands and my feet.' The two readings differ by one small letter. Some scholars prefer that reading, while the oldest translations read 'pierced.'

notes.meaning: His body is so stretched out and thin that he can count his bones. People stare at him and seem to enjoy his pain. On the cross, the hanging body made the bones stand out. The crowd looked on without pity.

They split up his clothes and gamble for his garment, as if he were already dead. At the cross the soldiers did exactly this (John 19:23-24). They divided his outer clothes into four parts and cast lots for his seamless inner robe. Such an exact fulfillment strengthens our faith that Jesus is the promised Savior.

After describing his trouble, he turns fully to God. He prays, 'Don't be far off,' and calls God 'my Strength.' He asks God to hurry, because time is short. Even when we feel weakest, we can still lean on God as our strength.

He begs to be saved from the sword, the dogs, the lion and the wild oxen, which are pictures of deadly enemies and, some say, of Satan. He calls his life 'precious', or literally 'my only one', because each of us has only one life and soul. Then the prayer suddenly turns: 'You have answered me!' For Jesus, the answer came not by escaping death but by being raised from it on the third day.

Sorrow now turns to praise. He promises to tell his 'brothers' about God's name, meaning who God is and what He has done. He will also praise God among the gathered people. Hebrews 2:12 gives these words to the risen Jesus, who calls his followers his brothers.

He calls everyone who fears the LORD to join his praise. To 'fear' God here means to honor Him with deep respect and awe. The descendants of Jacob and Israel are God's people. Christians have seen here the whole church, Jews and non-Jews together.

Here is the reason for praise. God did not turn away in disgust from the suffering one, or hide His face for good; He heard his cry. For Christians this means the Father accepted Jesus' suffering as full payment for sin. It also means no one in pain is turned away when they cry to Him.

He will praise God in the 'great assembly.' Even that praise comes as God's gift. He will keep his vows, the promises made to God in trouble, often kept by bringing a thank-offering. Christians read the great assembly as the worldwide church.

In Israel a thank-offering ended with a joyful meal, and the poor could be invited to share it. So here the humble eat and are filled, and those who seek God praise Him. 'May your hearts live forever' is like a host's blessing on his guests. Christians see Christ's sacrifice as the true feast that gives lasting life to those who trust him.

differ.view: The meal points naturally to the Lord's Supper, where Christ shares with us the fruits of his suffering.
The eating means feeding on Christ, the bread of life, by faith in the message of the gospel.

notes.meaning: The vision grows wider than Israel. People from the ends of the earth will remember God, turn to Him and worship Him. The reason is that the LORD is King and rules over every nation. Christians see here the gospel going out to all peoples.

Both the rich and powerful and the poor and dying will bow before God. 'Those who go down to the dust' are people facing death. No one can keep themselves alive, so rich and poor alike need the God who gives life. The wise thing is to trust our souls to Christ, who can keep them alive forever.
The praise of God will not die out. Each new generation will serve Him and tell the next about the Lord. God will always have a people in the world until the end of time.

Future believers will tell people not yet born about God's righteousness, His goodness and faithfulness in saving. Their message is simple: 'He has done it.' Salvation is God's own work, not ours. Some hear an echo here of Jesus' last words, 'It is finished.'
